title: vyshyvanka
summary: Vyshyvanka refers to the embroidered shirt integral to Ukrainian and Belarusian national costumes, characterized by unique regional embroidery styles. This garment serves not only as traditional attire but also as a symbol of cultural identity and patriotism in Ukraine.

sections.heading: Etymology
paragraphs: The term 'vyshyvanka' is derived from the [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] verb вишива́ти (vyshyvaty), meaning 'to embroider', combined with the noun-forming suffix -нка (-nka).

sections.heading: Ukrainian Vyshyvankas
paragraphs: Embroidery is a crucial aspect of the Ukrainian folk costume for both men and women. Ukrainian vyshyvankas are recognized for their distinctive embroidery styles that reflect the specific region of origin. Each piece of clothing can indicate the wearer's hometown, with various local techniques and color patterns rooted in the natural environment.

Historically, embroidery [[coal-in-ukraine|in Ukraine]] dates back to the 5th century B.C. as seen in [[scythians|Scythian]] art. The primary colors used in [[ukrainian-embroidery|Ukrainian embroidery]] are black, red, and white, while yellow, blue, and green serve as supplementary colors. Contemporary embroiderers strive to preserve traditional folk art techniques, as any alterations can diminish the value and authenticity of the work.

sections.heading: Cultural Significance
paragraphs: The vyshyvanka is imbued with cultural meanings, often regarded as a talisman that protects the wearer and narrates a story. The geometric patterns traditionally woven into the fabric are believed to safeguard individuals from harm. A common saying in Ukraine suggests that those born in a vyshyvanka are shielded by its maker.

The garment also holds patriotic significance, exemplified by figures such as Archduke Wilhelm of Austria, known as Vasyl Vyshyvanyi, who favored wearing the vyshyvanka. The Vyshyvanoho Square in [[lviv|Lviv]] is named in his honor.

sections.heading: Vyshyvanka Day
paragraphs: Vyshyvanka Day was established in 2006 by student Lesia Voroniuk at [[chernivtsi-university|Chernivtsi National University]] and has since evolved into an international celebration held on the third Thursday of May. This day aims to unite [[ukrainians|Ukrainians]] globally, regardless of their background, and is marked by wearing vyshyvankas to express national identity and patriotism.

In 2018, research by the Ministry of Economic Development and Trade of [[ukraine|Ukraine]] recognized 'Vyshyvanka Day' as a national holiday symbolizing Ukrainian consciousness and unity. The celebration involves participation from citizens, state authorities, and various organizations, promoting Ukrainian culture and traditions.

sections.heading: Influence on Fashion
paragraphs: In contemporary fashion, the vyshyvanka has gained international recognition. During Paris Fashion Week 2015, Ukrainian designer Vita Kin showcased modern interpretations of the vyshyvanka, merging traditional designs with contemporary aesthetics. This revival attracted attention from fashion icons and media outlets, with Vogue highlighting the garment's global appeal.

The vyshyvanka has been embraced by various public figures, including French actress Melanie Thierry and Queen Máxima of the Netherlands, further solidifying its status as a fashionable item beyond [[eastern-europe|Eastern Europe]].
